claim: Meis2 mRNA was first detected at embryonic day (E) 11.5 in a restricted group of large DRG neurons in mouse.
source: In mouse, Meis2 mRNA was first detected at embryonic day (E) 11.5 in a restricted group of large DRG neurons.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation from in situ hybridization experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Meis2 restricted expression pattern was maintained at E14.5, E18.5, and adult stages in mouse.
source: This restricted expression pattern was maintained at E14.5, E18.5, and adult stages (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and references Figure 1A showing ISH data across developmental stages.

claim: In chick, Meis2 was expressed in most DRG neurons at Hamburger–Hamilton stage (HH) 24.
source: In chick, Meis2 was expressed in most DRG neurons at Hamburger–Hamilton stage (HH) 24, but later becomes restricted to a well-defined subpopulation in the ventrolateral part of the DRG where LTMRs and proprioceptors are located (Rifkin et al., 2000; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation from ISH experiments in chick embryos, with citation to Rifkin et al., 2000.

claim: Meis2 expression in chick later becomes restricted to a well-defined subpopulation in the ventrolateral part of the DRG where LTMRs and proprioceptors are located.
source: In chick, Meis2 was expressed in most DRG neurons at Hamburger–Hamilton stage (HH) 24, but later becomes restricted to a well-defined subpopulation in the ventrolateral part of the DRG where LTMRs and proprioceptors are located (Rifkin et al., 2000; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation with reference to published literature (Rifkin et al., 2000) and supporting figure.

claim: Meis2-positive cells expressed the pan-neuronal marker Islet1 in both mouse and chick.
source: In both species, Meis2-positive cells also expressed the pan-neuronal marker Islet1, indicating that they are postmitotic neurons.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this co-expression observation from ISH combined with immunofluorescence.

claim: Meis2-positive cells are postmitotic neurons.
source: In both species, Meis2-positive cells also expressed the pan-neuronal marker Islet1, indicating that they are postmitotic neurons.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the co-expression with Islet1, a known marker of postmitotic neurons.

claim: Meis2-positive cells represented about 15% of Islet1-positive DRG neurons at HH29 and HH36 in chick.
source: In chick, we estimated that Meis2-positive cells represented about 15% of Islet1-positive DRG neurons at HH29 and HH36, respectively, suggesting a stable expression in given neuronal populations during embryonic development.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data from cell counting in chick embryos.

claim: Meis2 expression is stable in given neuronal populations during embryonic development in chick.
source: In chick, we estimated that Meis2-positive cells represented about 15% of Islet1-positive DRG neurons at HH29 and HH36, respectively, suggesting a stable expression in given neuronal populations during embryonic development.
evidence: The manuscript infers stable expression from the similar percentages at two developmental stages.

claim: Double ISH for Meis2 and Ntrk2, Ntrk3 or Ret mRNAs in E14.5 and E18.5 mouse embryonic DRG showed a large co-expression in Ntrk2- and Ntrk3-positive neurons.
source: Double ISH for Meis2 and Ntrk2, Ntrk3 or Ret mRNAs in E14.5 and E18.5 mouse embryonic DRG (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B) showed a large co-expression in Ntrk2- and Ntrk3-positive neurons confirming that Meis2-positive neurons belong to the LTMR and proprioceptive subpopulations.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from double ISH experiments shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Meis2-positive neurons belong to the LTMR and proprioceptive subpopulations.
source: Double ISH for Meis2 and Ntrk2, Ntrk3 or Ret mRNAs in E14.5 and E18.5 mouse embryonic DRG (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B) showed a large co-expression in Ntrk2- and Ntrk3-positive neurons confirming that Meis2-positive neurons belong to the LTMR and proprioceptive subpopulations.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from co-expression with known markers of these populations.

claim: Virtually all large Ret-positive neurons representing part of the LTMR pool co-expressed Meis2 at E14.5 before the emergence of the small nociceptive Ret-positive population.
source: Finally, double ISH for Meis2 and Ret in E14.5 mouse DRG showed that virtually all large Ret-positive neurons representing part of the LTMR pool co-expressed Meis2 at this stage before the emergence of the small nociceptive Ret-positive population.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from double ISH experiments.

claim: 30.5 ± 3.5% of Meis2-positive neurons co-expressed Ntrk2 at P7.
source: We estimated that 30.5 ± 3.5% (mean ± SEM; n = 3) of Meis2-positive neurons co-expressed Ntrk2, and that 39.5 ± 5.4% co-expressed Ntrk3.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data from immunofluorescence experiments at P7.

claim: 39.5 ± 5.4% of Meis2-positive neurons co-expressed Ntrk3 at P7.
source: We estimated that 30.5 ± 3.5% (mean ± SEM; n = 3) of Meis2-positive neurons co-expressed Ntrk2, and that 39.5 ± 5.4% co-expressed Ntrk3.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data from immunofluorescence experiments at P7.

claim: Meis2 was co-expressed in 53.6 ± 9.4% of Ntrk2-positive neurons at P7.
source: Conversely, Meis2 was co-expressed in 53.6 ± 9.4% of Ntrk2-positive neurons, and in 78.5 ± 5.0% of Ntrk3-positive neurons.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data from immunofluorescence experiments at P7.

claim: Meis2 was co-expressed in 78.5 ± 5.0% of Ntrk3-positive neurons at P7.
source: Conversely, Meis2 was co-expressed in 53.6 ± 9.4% of Ntrk2-positive neurons, and in 78.5 ± 5.0% of Ntrk3-positive neurons.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data from immunofluorescence experiments at P7.

claim: Only a few Meis2-positive neurons co-expressed Ntrk1 at E11.5 and E18.5 in mouse.
source: In mouse, comparison of Meis2 mRNA expression to Ntrk1, a well-established marker for early nociceptive and thermo-sensitive neurons, showed that only a few Meis2-positive neurons co-expressed Ntrk1 at E11.5 and E18.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from ISH combined with immunofluorescence.

claim: Meis2 expression was fully excluded from the Ntrk1 subpopulation in chick HH29 embryos.
source: In chick HH29 embryos, Meis2 expression was fully excluded from the Ntrk1 subpopulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from ISH combined with immunofluorescence in chick.

claim: In adult mouse DRG, Meis2-expressing neurons are largely excluded from the nociceptive and thermosensitive populations.
source: In adult mouse DRG, comparison of Meis2 mRNA to Ntrk1, Calca, and TrpV1 immunostaining confirmed that Meis2-expressing neurons are largely excluded from the nociceptive and thermosensitive populations of DRG neurons.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from ISH combined with immunofluorescence in adult mice.

claim: A large proportion of Meis2-positive neurons co-expressed Nefh in adult mouse DRG.
source: Instead, a large proportion of Meis2-positive neurons co-expressed Nefh, a marker for large myelinated neurons including LTMR and proprioceptors, and Pvalb, a specific marker for proprioceptors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from ISH combined with immunofluorescence in adult mice.

claim: A large proportion of Meis2-positive neurons co-expressed Pvalb in adult mouse DRG.
source: Instead, a large proportion of Meis2-positive neurons co-expressed Nefh, a marker for large myelinated neurons including LTMR and proprioceptors, and Pvalb, a specific marker for proprioceptors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from ISH combined with immunofluorescence in adult mice.

claim: Many retrogradely labeled sensory neurons from skin were immunopositive for Meis2, Maf, Ntrk2, and Ntrk3.
source: Analyses of CTB expression in lumbar DRG 3 d later at P8 showed that many retrogradely labeled sensory neurons were also immunopositive for Meis2, Maf, Ntrk2, and Ntrk3 (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from retrograde tracing experiments combined with immunofluorescence.

claim: Meis2 expression is restricted to the Aβ-field, Aβ-SA1 and Aβ-RA subclasses of LTMR neurons and proprioceptive neurons.
source: Altogether, our results on Meis2 co-localization with Nefh, Ntrk2, Ntrk3, Ret, Pvalb, and Maf at different embryonic and postnatal stages are consistent with previous reports on restricted Meis2 expression to the Aβ-field, Aβ-SA1 and Aβ-RA subclasses of LTMR neurons and proprioceptive neurons (Sharma et al., 2020; Usoskin et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on their data and cites previous publications.

claim: The relatively lower coincidence of Meis2 and Ntrk2 expressions compared to Ntrk3 is consistent with Meis2 being excluded from the Aδ-LTMRs (D-hair mechanoreceptors).
source: The relatively lower coincidence of Meis2 and Ntrk2 expressions compared to Ntrk3 is consistent with Meis2 being excluded from the Aδ-LTMRs (D-hair mechanoreceptors).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the quantitative co-expression data.

claim: The lack of co-expression with Ntrk1 and TrpV1 confirmed Meis2 exclusion from peptidergic and non-peptidergic subpopulations.
source: The lack of co-expression with Ntrk1 and TrpV1 also confirmed Meis2 exclusion from peptidergic and non-peptidergic subpopulations.
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on their co-expression data.

claim: About 65% of Meis2-positive neurons were lost on the ablated side compared to the contralateral side in HH36 embryos following limb bud ablation.
source: In HH36 embryos, about 65% of Meis2-positive neurons were lost on the ablated side compared to the contralateral side (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data from limb ablation experiments in chick.

claim: About 30% of all sensory DRG neurons represented by the pan-neuronal marker Islet1 were lost following limb ablation in HH36 embryos.
source: This is consistent with a 30% loss of all sensory DRG neurons represented by the pan-neuronal marker Islet1, and the 50 and 65% loss of Ntrk2 and Ntrk3-positive VL-neurons, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data from limb ablation experiments in chick.

claim: 50% of Ntrk2-positive VL-neurons were lost following limb ablation in HH36 embryos.
source: This is consistent with a 30% loss of all sensory DRG neurons represented by the pan-neuronal marker Islet1, and the 50 and 65% loss of Ntrk2 and Ntrk3-positive VL-neurons, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data from limb ablation experiments in chick.

claim: 65% of Ntrk3-positive VL-neurons were lost following limb ablation in HH36 embryos.
source: This is consistent with a 30% loss of all sensory DRG neurons represented by the pan-neuronal marker Islet1, and the 50 and 65% loss of Ntrk2 and Ntrk3-positive VL-neurons, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data from limb ablation experiments in chick.

claim: The number of Ntrk2-positive DL neurons was not significantly affected by limb ablation in HH36 embryos.
source: The number of Ntrk2-positive DL neurons was not significantly affected.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from limb ablation experiments in chick.

claim: In HH27 embryos, no significant loss of Islet1-positive neurons was detected following limb ablation.
source: In HH27 embryos, while no significant loss of Islet1-positive neurons was detected following limb ablation, about 40% of Meis2-positive neurons were lost, and remaining Meis2-positive neurons expressed very low levels of Meis2 mRNAs (Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data from limb ablation experiments in chick.

claim: About 40% of Meis2-positive neurons were lost following limb ablation in HH27 embryos.
source: In HH27 embryos, while no significant loss of Islet1-positive neurons was detected following limb ablation, about 40% of Meis2-positive neurons were lost, and remaining Meis2-positive neurons expressed very low levels of Meis2 mRNAs (Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data from limb ablation experiments in chick.

claim: Remaining Meis2-positive neurons expressed very low levels of Meis2 mRNAs following limb ablation in HH27 embryos.
source: In HH27 embryos, while no significant loss of Islet1-positive neurons was detected following limb ablation, about 40% of Meis2-positive neurons were lost, and remaining Meis2-positive neurons expressed very low levels of Meis2 mRNAs (Figure 1D).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from limb ablation experiments in chick.

claim: Target-derived signals are necessary for the maintenance but not the induction of Meis2 expression in sensory neurons.
source: These results indicate that target-derived signals are necessary for the maintenance but not the induction of Meis2 expression in sensory neurons.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this from the limb ablation experiments showing loss of Meis2 expression after initial induction.

claim: Wnt1Cre::Meis2LoxP/LoxP newborn pups exhibited a cleft palate.
source: This crossing efficiently inactivated Meis2 in the neural crest, and Wnt1Cre::Meis2LoxP/LoxP newborn pups exhibited a cleft palate as previously reported in another conditional Meis2 mouse strain (Machon et al., 2015; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and cites previous work reporting the same phenotype.

claim: Wnt1Cre::Meis2LoxP/LoxP newborn pups were not viable.
source: They were, however, not viable, precluding functional and anatomical analyses at adult stages.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation.

claim: Isl1Cre/+::Meis2LoxP/LoxP mutant pups were viable and appeared healthy.
source: Mutant pups were viable, appeared healthy, and displayed a normal palate, allowing sensory behavior investigations.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation.

claim: Isl1Cre/+::Meis2LoxP/LoxP mutant pups displayed a normal palate.
source: Mutant pups were viable, appeared healthy, and displayed a normal palate, allowing sensory behavior investigations.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation.

claim: The frequency of withdrawal responses to Von Frey filaments was significantly decreased in Isl1+/Cre::Meis2LoxP/LoxP mice compared to control WT and Isl1+/Cre mice between 0.16 and 0.6 g.
source: We used Von Frey filaments to apply a series of low forces ranging from 0.008 to 1.4 g to the hind paw and found the frequency of withdrawal responses to be significantly decreased in Isl1+/Cre::Meis2LoxP/LoxP mice compared to control WT and Isl1+/Cre mice between 0.16 and 0.6 g (Figure 1E), indicating that mutant mice are less responsive to light touch.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative behavioral data from Von Frey testing.

claim: Isl1+/Cre::Meis2LoxP/LoxP mutant mice are less responsive to light touch.
source: We used Von Frey filaments to apply a series of low forces ranging from 0.008 to 1.4 g to the hind paw and found the frequency of withdrawal responses to be significantly decreased in Isl1+/Cre::Meis2LoxP/LoxP mice compared to control WT and Isl1+/Cre mice between 0.16 and 0.6 g (Figure 1E), indicating that mutant mice are less responsive to light touch.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the Von Frey behavioral data.

claim: No differences were observed between WT and Isl1+/Cre mice for any of the Von Frey stimuli applied.
source: No differences were observed between WT and Isl1+/Cre mice for any of the stimuli applied.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from Von Frey testing.

claim: Responses in the cotton swab dynamic touch assay were significantly decreased in Isl1+/Cre::Meis2LoxP/LoxP mice compared to control WT and Isl1+/Cre littermates.
source: Behaviors evoked from stimulation of the glabrous skin were next assessed using the 'cotton swab' dynamic touch assay (Bourane et al., 2015). Here, responses were significantly decreased in Isl1+/Cre::Meis2LoxP/LoxP mice compared to control WT and Isl1+/Cre littermates (Figure 1F).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative behavioral data from the cotton swab test, with citation to the method.

claim: No difference in response latencies was found between WT, Isl1Cre/+ and Isl1Cre/+::Meis2LoxP/LoxP mice in the hot plate assay.
source: We also used the hot plate assay to assess noxious heat-evoked behaviors and found no difference in response latencies between WT, Isl1Cre/+ and Isl1Cre/+::Meis2LoxP/LoxP mice (Figure 1G).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative behavioral data from the hot plate test.

claim: Bouts of behavior in the sticky tape test were significantly reduced in Isl1Cre/+::Meis2LoxP/LoxP mice compared to WT and Isl1Cre/+ control mice.
source: Finally, we compared the sensitivity of mice to stimuli applied to the hairy skin using the sticky tape test. Placing sticky tape on the back skin evoked attempts to remove the stimulus in a defined time window, and we found that such bouts of behavior were significantly reduced in Isl1Cre/+::Meis2LoxP/LoxP mice compared to WT and Isl1Cre/+ control mice (Figure 1H).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative behavioral data from the sticky tape test.

claim: No obvious motor deficits were observed in Isl1Cre/+::Meis2LoxP/LoxP mice.
source: Finally, although Meis2 and Isl1 are both expressed by spinal motor neurons and proprioceptors (Catela et al., 2016; Dasen et al., 2005; Ericson et al., 1992), we did not observe obvious motor deficits in Isl1Cre/+::Meis2LoxP/LoxP mice.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation with citations to previous work on Meis2 and Isl1 expression.

claim: No differences in any of the gait parameters measured were found between WT and Isl1Cre/+::Meis2LoxP/LoxP mutant mice in catwalk analysis.
source: Thus, in a catwalk analysis we found no differences in any of the gait parameters measured between WT and mutant mice (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from catwalk analysis.

claim: Meis2 gene inactivation specifically affects light touch sensation both in the glabrous and the hairy skin.
source: Overall, these behavioral analyses indicate that Meis2 gene inactivation specifically affects light touch sensation both in the glabrous and the hairy skin.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this from the behavioral data showing deficits in light touch but not noxious heat responses.

claim: Meis2 gene activity is necessary for the anatomical and functional maturation of LTMRs.
source: The impaired behavioral response to light touch in Meis2 mutant suggests that Meis2 gene activity is necessary for the anatomical and functional maturation of LTMRs.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the behavioral deficits observed in mutant mice.

claim: There was no difference in the size of the DRGs between E16.5 WT and Isl1Cre/+::Meis2LoxP/LoxP embryos.
source: There was no difference in the size of the DRGs between E16.5 WT and Isl1Cre/+::Meis2LoxP/LoxP embryos as well as in the number of Ntrk2 and Ntrk3-positive neurons (Figure 2A), suggesting no cell loss.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative histological data from E16.5 embryos.

claim: There was no difference in the number of Ntrk2 and Ntrk3-positive neurons between E16.5 WT and Isl1Cre/+::Meis2LoxP/LoxP embryos.
source: There was no difference in the size of the DRGs between E16.5 WT and Isl1Cre/+::Meis2LoxP/LoxP embryos as well as in the number of Ntrk2 and Ntrk3-positive neurons (Figure 2A), suggesting no cell loss.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative histological data from E16.5 embryos.

claim: The number of LTMR and proprioceptors identified as positive for Ntrk2, Ntrk3, Ret, and Maf was unchanged following Meis2 inactivation in E18.5 embryonic DRGs.
source: In E18.5 embryonic DRGs, the number of LTMR and proprioceptors identified as positive for Ntrk2, Ntrk3, Ret, and Maf was unchanged following Meis2 inactivation (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative histological data from E18.5 embryos.

claim: The number of Ntrk1-positive neurons was unaffected by Meis2 inactivation.
source: Consistent with the lack of Meis2 expression in nociceptors, the number of Ntrk1-positive neurons was also unaffected (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative histological data.

claim: Quantification of DRG neuron populations at P0 in Wnt1Cre::Meis2LoxP/LoxP mice showed no differences in the number of Ntrk2 and Ntrk3-positive neurons.
source: Finally, quantification of DRG neuron populations at P0 in Wnt1Cre::Meis2LoxP/LoxP mice showed similar results with no differences in the number of Ntrk2 and Ntrk3-positive neurons (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative histological data from P0 mice.

claim: Phospho-Creb (pCreb) expression in Ntrk2 and Ntrk3-positive neurons was similar in WT and mutants at P0.
source: At this stage, phospho-Creb (pCreb) expression in Ntrk2 and Ntrk3-positive neurons was similar in WT and mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Ntrk signaling is not affected.
evidence: The manuscript provides immunofluorescence data from P0 mice.

claim: Ntrk signaling is not affected by Meis2 inactivation.
source: At this stage, phospho-Creb (pCreb) expression in Ntrk2 and Ntrk3-positive neurons was similar in WT and mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Ntrk signaling is not affected.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the pCreb expression data.

claim: Meis2 is dispensable for LTMR and proprioceptor survival and specification during embryogenesis.
source: Altogether, these results show that Meis2 is dispensable for LTMR and proprioceptor survival and specification during embryogenesis.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this from the histological data showing no loss of neurons or changes in marker expression.

claim: RNAseq analysis identified 43 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the WT vs Isl1+/Cre::Meis2LoxP/LoxP comparison.
source: Analyses of the dataset (n = 3; p<0.05; Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—source data 1) identified 43 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the WT vs Isl1+/Cre::Meis2LoxP/LoxP comparison, 107 DEGs in the Isl1+/Cre vs Isl1+/Cre::Meis2LoxP/LoxP comparison, and 109 DEGs in the WT vs Isl1+/Cre comparison.

claim: Eight of the 10 best DEGs were found to be expressed in sensory neurons expressing Meis2.
source: Half of them were down- or upregulated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), and eight were found to be expressed in sensory neurons expressing Meis2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from comparison with single-cell RNAseq data.

claim: The 10 best DEGs include three ncRNA (A230077H06Rik, Gm20163, Gm42418).
source: These include three ncRNA (A230077H06Rik, Gm20163, Gm42418), the Adhesion G Protein-Coupled Receptor G3 (Adgrg3, also known as GPR97), the Cellular Repressor of E1A Stimulated Genes 2 (Creg2), predicted to be located in Golgi apparatus and endoplasmic reticulum, the Tubulin Alpha 8 (Tuba8) mutated in Polymicrogyria, a developmental malformation of the cortex (Abdollahi et al., 2009), the Hes Family BHLH Transcription Factor 5 (Hes5) activated downstream of the Notch pathway and largely involved in neuronal differentiation, the mitochondrial ribosomal protein s28 (Mrps28) whose mutation severely impairs the development of the nervous system (Pulman et al., 2019), the Phospholipase C Delta 1 (Plcd1) important for neuronal development and function of mature neurons, and the Pyridoxamine 5'-Phosphate Oxidase (Pnpo) involved in the synthesis of vitamin B6 and whose mutation causes a form of neonatal epileptic encephalopathy and motor neuron disease.
evidence: The manuscript lists these genes as part of the 10 best DEGs.
